cards.text: David, king of Israel, wrote this song when he fled from his own son, Absalom. His OWN son, friend. And David skips the small talk and takes his problem straight to the LORD.

cards.question: David is on the run, and he tells the LORD how his ___ have increased.

cards.text: And it's not just how many are rising up against him. Running from your own son is bad enough, and NOW people are talking about you too.

cards.question: Many are rising up against David. What are they saying about him?

answers.text: His own men will turn on him
His throne is gone for good

cards.text: Then, BOOM, the whole song turns on one little word: "But." David stops staring at the crowd and looks at the LORD instead.

cards.question: Enemies are rising up all around David. What does David call the LORD, all around him?
With many saying God won't deliver him, David calls the LORD the One who lifts his head.

cards.text: Then David says it plain: he cries aloud to the LORD. Not a whisper, friend. ALOUD.

cards.question: When David cries aloud to the LORD, the LORD stays silent.

cards.text: Now get this: David lies down and sleeps, and he wakes again, while he's on the RUN. Me? I lay awake for years in that junk drawer, and the only thing after me was dust.

cards.question: David sleeps and wakes again with enemies rising up against him. Why, according to David?

cards.text: And the enemies? David calls them myriads, set against him on every side. That's the last cookie on the tray when the whole kitchen walks in.

cards.question: Surrounded on every side, David says he will not ___ the myriads set against him.

cards.text: Then David stops describing his trouble and starts asking, and he is NOT whispering.

cards.question: David cries, "Arise, O LORD!" What does he ask God to do for him?
David asks God to strike all his enemies on the jaw and break the teeth of the wicked.

cards.text: Then David wraps up the whole song with one big truth and one last prayer.

cards.question: To close his song, David says salvation belongs to the ___.
David ends his song by praying for a blessing on himself and no one else.

findings.problem: "Then David stops describing his trouble and starts asking" misdescribes the flow. Verses 3 to 6 are declarations of trust (shield, sleep, no fear), not a description of trouble. David already cried aloud to the LORD in verse 4, which card 8 told, so verse 7 is not where he "starts asking."

rule.text: Noticing. What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "strong" is an adjective, while "LORD" and "king" are nouns naming who someone is. The answers are not the same kind of thing, so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The right answer "God will not deliver him" is the only one that mentions God, and "deliver" is the only Bible-sounding word. In a psalm, that makes the right answer stand out from "His own men will turn on him" and "His throne is gone for good."

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: Most story cards (3, 5, 8, 14, 17) are plain narration with mild energy. Only cards 10 and 12 carry a real joke. The walkthrough reads like a nice dad being pleasant, not laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
